subtopic_detail: Widespread umbilicated papules with one inflamed crusted lesion in a well six year old with normal skin elsewhere
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a six year old boy whose parents want his spots removed. They have spread over four months from his left flank to his trunk and arms, and the school swimming teacher has told the family he should stay out of the pool until they are gone.

One lesion on his forearm became red and crusted last week and is now smaller than it was. He is otherwise well, plays normally and takes no regular medicines.

data_table.Examination: Approximately thirty dome shaped pearly papules two to four millimetres across with central umbilication, scattered over the left flank, trunk and both forearms, one lesion on the right forearm red and crusted with surrounding erythema of three millimetres and no fluctuance, skin between lesions normal without eczema, no regional lymphadenopathy, no lesions on the eyelids or genitals

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Explain the natural course, advise covering lesions for contact sport, and confirm he may continue swimming lessons
options.rationale: Molluscum contagiosum in an immunocompetent child resolves spontaneously over months to a couple of years, and active treatment is painful, may scar and does not shorten the course meaningfully. Exclusion from school or swimming is not recommended, and covering lesions during close contact activities is the proportionate measure. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Molluscum contagiosum)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Molluscum contagiosum

options.text: Refer him for cryotherapy to each lesion, with repeat treatments every three weeks until the lesions have cleared
options.rationale: Cryotherapy is painful, poorly tolerated by young children and risks hypopigmentation and scarring, and thirty lesions would require several sessions for a condition that resolves without treatment. It is occasionally offered to older patients with a few troublesome lesions. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Molluscum contagiosum)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Molluscum contagiosum

options.text: Arrange curettage of the lesions under general anaesthesia, with topical anaesthetic applied before the procedure
options.rationale: A general anaesthetic to remove a self limiting viral skin infection exposes the child to more risk than the condition carries, and new lesions commonly appear afterwards through autoinoculation. Curettage has a role only for a small number of persistent disfiguring lesions in an older child. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Molluscum contagiosum)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Molluscum contagiosum

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin for five days to treat the inflamed forearm lesion and the surrounding area of erythema
options.rationale: A single molluscum lesion that becomes red, tender and crusted before shrinking usually reflects the host immune response that precedes resolution rather than bacterial infection, and this lesion is already involuting. Antibiotics are reserved for spreading cellulitis with expanding erythema, fever or systemic upset. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Prescribe topical imiquimod cream three nights per week and review the response to treatment after twelve weeks
options.rationale: Randomised evidence in children shows imiquimod is no better than vehicle for molluscum while causing application site reactions, and it is not recommended for this indication. Its established uses are genital warts and some keratinocyte cancers in adults. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Molluscum contagiosum)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Molluscum contagiosum

explanation.summary: Molluscum contagiosum is a poxvirus infection of the skin that spreads by direct contact and autoinoculation, and in healthy children it clears spontaneously, usually within twelve to eighteen months although occasionally longer. Lesions are pearly dome shaped papules with a central dimple, and an individual lesion that becomes red, swollen and crusted is most often undergoing immune mediated resolution, a phenomenon families find alarming unless it is explained in advance. Australian guidance does not support exclusion from school, childcare or swimming, and children should not be kept out of the pool, although lesions are covered for contact sports and towels are not shared. Treatments including cryotherapy, curettage, cantharidin and imiquimod carry pain, pigment change or scarring and have limited evidence of benefit in children. Extensive or atypical disease, particularly with facial or genital involvement outside the usual pattern, prompts consideration of underlying immunodeficiency or of coexisting atopic dermatitis that facilitates spread.
key_points: Molluscum resolves spontaneously in immunocompetent children, usually within twelve to eighteen months.
Exclusion from school, childcare or swimming is not recommended; lesions are covered for close contact activities.
An inflamed crusted lesion that is shrinking usually signals immune clearance rather than bacterial infection.
Cryotherapy, curettage and imiquimod carry pain, pigmentary change or scarring without meaningfully shortening the illness.
Coexisting eczema promotes spread, so treating the dermatitis reduces autoinoculation.
explanation.pearls: The red crusted lesion that worries parents, sometimes called the beginning of the end sign, predicts clearance of the whole eruption within the following weeks to months and is a useful piece of anticipatory explanation at the first consultation.

sources.label: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Molluscum contagiosum
Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews: Interventions for cutaneous molluscum contagiosum

subtopic_detail: Repetitive vomiting with pallor and lethargy two hours after a first exposure to rice cereal in a six month old
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar called to a six month old boy brought in by ambulance. He vomited repeatedly about two hours after his mother gave him rice cereal for the first time this morning, and by the eighth vomit he had gone grey and floppy in her arms.

He has been exclusively breastfed until this week and has eczema that is well controlled with emollients. He has had no fever, no cough and no loose stools, and his immunisations are up to date. His skin has stayed clear through the episode and his breathing has been quiet throughout.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 178 beats per minute, blood pressure 68/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 44 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 36.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pale and hypotonic but rousable, capillary refill four seconds centrally, cool peripheries to the wrists and ankles, dry mucous membranes, no urticaria, angio-oedema or flushing anywhere on the skin, chest clear with no wheeze or stridor, abdomen soft with no distension or mass, anterior fontanelle sunken
data_table.Investigations: Venous blood gas pH 7.28, bicarbonate 16 mmol/L (22 to 32), lactate 3.1 mmol/L (less than 2), blood glucose 4.2 mmol/L (3.5 to 6.0)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Give intramuscular adrenaline 150 micrograms into the lateral thigh and repeat the dose after 5 minutes if needed
options.rationale: Adrenaline is the treatment for anaphylaxis, which requires acute skin or mucosal features with respiratory or cardiovascular compromise, or sudden hypotension after exposure to a known allergen, and it typically begins within minutes rather than two hours. This boy has profound vomiting with shock, no skin involvement and no airway signs, which is the non immunoglobulin E mediated pattern that does not respond to adrenaline. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome

options.text: Take blood cultures and give intravenous ceftriaxone now, with a fluid bolus once the antibiotic has been administered
options.rationale: Sepsis is the usual initial working diagnosis in this presentation and antibiotics are defensible when the picture is unclear, but this child is afebrile with a clear temporal link to a first food exposure and a normal respiratory and abdominal examination. Fluid resuscitation is still the first priority even when antibiotics are given. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on sepsis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on sepsis

options.text: Give an intravenous bolus of 20 mL/kg of 0.9 per cent sodium chloride and a single intravenous dose of ondansetron
options.rationale: Acute food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome causes massive fluid shift into the gut, and around fifteen per cent of episodes present in shock, so isotonic crystalloid resuscitation is the intervention that reverses the physiology. A single dose of ondansetron shortens the vomiting in children over six months and is now standard in acute episodes. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome

options.text: Give a stat oral dose of prednisolone 1 mg/kg and observe him for 4 hours before securing intravenous access
options.rationale: An orally administered drug is futile in a child who is vomiting repeatedly and shocked, and corticosteroid has no established role in reversing the acute fluid shift of this syndrome. Deferring intravenous access for four hours in a shocked infant risks deterioration. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome

options.text: Arrange skin prick testing to rice and cow milk protein today and discharge him with an adrenaline autoinjector and a plan
options.rationale: Skin prick and specific immunoglobulin E testing are typically negative in this condition because the mechanism is cell mediated, so a negative result would falsely reassure and a positive one would mislead. Testing is a question for the allergy clinic after resuscitation, not an immediate intervention in a shocked infant. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome

explanation.summary: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome is a non immunoglobulin E mediated food allergy that presents with profuse repetitive vomiting one to four hours after ingestion of the trigger, often with pallor, lethargy and sometimes shock, and characteristically without any skin or respiratory features. Rice, cow milk, soy, oat and egg are the commonest Australian triggers, and the first recognised episode frequently follows the very first exposure to a new solid. Because the mechanism is cell mediated, skin prick tests and specific immunoglobulin E are usually negative and the diagnosis rests on the history and the reproducible timing. Acute treatment is isotonic fluid resuscitation with ondansetron, and adrenaline has no role unless the picture is genuinely anaphylactic. Ongoing care involves strict avoidance of the trigger, a written acute action plan for emergency departments that names the syndrome, and supervised oral food challenge to assess tolerance, which develops in most children by three to five years of age.
key_points: The hallmark is repetitive vomiting one to four hours after ingestion, with pallor and lethargy and without urticaria or wheeze.
Around fifteen per cent of acute episodes present with hypovolaemic shock, and isotonic crystalloid is the treatment.
Ondansetron shortens acute episodes in children over six months and is used alongside fluids.
Skin prick tests and specific immunoglobulin E are usually negative because the reaction is cell mediated.
Most children outgrow the syndrome by three to five years, confirmed by supervised oral food challenge.
explanation.pearls: The single most useful discriminator at the bedside is timing with an absence of skin signs: anaphylaxis begins within minutes and involves skin or mucosa in about eighty per cent of cases, whereas this syndrome begins one to four hours after the meal and leaves the skin entirely clear.

sources.label: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on sepsis
BMJ Best Practice: Non IgE mediated food allergy

subtopic_detail: Episodes of back arching and head turning during and after feeds in a thriving four month old who stays alert
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a four month old girl referred by her general practitioner with possible seizures. Her mother describes episodes in which the baby suddenly arches her back, turns her head to the right and stiffens for up to a minute, then relaxes and carries on.

The episodes happen during a feed or within about twenty minutes of finishing one, up to six times a day, and never while she is asleep. Through each episode she keeps her eyes open and watches her mother, and she settles immediately when picked up and held upright. She brings up small amounts of milk after most feeds, and her weight has tracked along the 25th centile since birth.

data_table.Examination: Alert and socially responsive, smiles and vocalises, follows across the midline, head control appropriate for age with no head lag beyond expected, tone and power symmetrical in all four limbs, deep tendon reflexes normal and symmetrical, anterior fontanelle soft and flat, head circumference on the 25th centile tracking parallel to the centile lines, no dysmorphic features, abdomen soft with no organomegaly

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange an urgent electroencephalogram and review her in the neurology clinic once the recording has been reported
options.rationale: An electroencephalogram is the right investigation when the events are stereotyped clusters with impaired awareness, developmental regression or occurrence during sleep, none of which fit episodes that arise only around feeds in a fully alert infant. Ordering it first tends to prolong uncertainty and invites over interpretation of normal infant variants. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants

options.text: Advise upright positioning after feeds with smaller more frequent volumes, and review her in two weeks to reassess
options.rationale: Dystonic posturing that is tightly time locked to feeds, preserves awareness and abates on being held upright is the recognised reflux associated movement pattern, and conservative feeding measures both treat it and confirm the diagnosis when the episodes settle. Review is built in so that failure to improve triggers reconsideration rather than open ended reassurance. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants

options.text: Commence oral levetiracetam at a weight based starting dose and arrange review in the general paediatric clinic
options.rationale: Starting an antiepileptic drug commits an infant to treatment and monitoring for events that are not epileptic, and it will not change episodes driven by oesophageal acid exposure. Antiepileptic treatment follows a diagnosis of epilepsy rather than preceding it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology

options.text: Request magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and cervical spine under general anaesthesia to exclude a structural lesion
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated for a fixed head tilt that does not correct, for focal neurological signs, for an abnormally growing head, or for developmental regression, whereas this infant has symmetrical tone, normal development and head circumference tracking along her centile. Anaesthetising a thriving four month old for a pattern explained by feeding is not justified. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on torticollis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on torticollis

options.text: Arrange an upper gastrointestinal contrast study to document reflux and to quantify the extent of oesophageal exposure
options.rationale: A contrast study assesses anatomy such as malrotation and strictures but is poor at quantifying reflux, with both false positives and false negatives, and it delivers radiation to answer a question a therapeutic trial answers better. It earns its place when bilious vomiting or a suspected obstruction is in play. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants

explanation.summary: Sandifer syndrome is the association of gastro-oesophageal reflux with paroxysmal dystonic posturing, most often back arching with lateral head rotation, and it is a common reason for infants to be referred with suspected seizures. The features that separate it from epilepsy are its relationship to feeds, complete preservation of awareness and responsiveness during the event, immediate relief with upright positioning, and a normal interictal neurological examination. Infants are typically thriving, so failure to gain weight, haematemesis, bilious vomiting or a bulging fontanelle should redirect the assessment. Management is the standard conservative approach to infant reflux, with positional measures, smaller more frequent feeds and consideration of thickened feeds or a trial of an extensively hydrolysed formula when cow milk protein allergy is suspected. Acid suppression is reserved for infants with clear complications of reflux rather than for posturing alone, because proton pump inhibitors in infants carry risks of gastroenteritis and lower respiratory infection without good evidence of benefit for these episodes.
key_points: Dystonic posturing tightly linked to feeds with preserved awareness is the signature of reflux associated posturing, not of seizures.
Relief on being held upright and absence of events during sleep are strong negative predictors of epilepsy.
A normal interictal examination with age appropriate development and normal head growth argues against structural pathology.
Conservative feeding measures both treat the problem and serve as a diagnostic trial with planned review.
Poor weight gain, haematemesis, bilious vomiting or neurological signs move the child out of this pathway.
explanation.pearls: Infantile spasms are the seizure type that must not be missed at this age: they occur in clusters of brief symmetrical flexion or extension movements, classically on waking rather than around feeds, and they warrant an electroencephalogram within days because treatment delay worsens developmental outcome.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on torticollis

subtopic_detail: Progressive pallor after a viral illness in a well two year old with isolated anaemia and a low reticulocyte count
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a two year old boy whose childcare educators told his parents he looked washed out. Four weeks ago he had a week of fever and a runny nose that settled without treatment.

His parents say he has been a little quieter than usual in the last fortnight but still runs around the yard and eats his meals. He drinks about 400 mL of cow milk a day and eats meat three times a week. He takes no medicines, and his urine and stools have been their usual colour.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae and pale palmar creases, alert and playing in the cubicle, soft systolic flow murmur at the left sternal edge, no hepatomegaly or splenomegaly, no lymphadenopathy, no bruising, petechiae or bony tenderness, no jaundice
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 64 g/L (105 to 135), mean cell volume 78 fL (70 to 86), reticulocytes 8 x10^9/L (20 to 100), white cell count 7.4 x10^9/L (5.0 to 15.0) with neutrophils 3.1 x10^9/L, platelets 342 x10^9/L (150 to 450), blood film shows normochromic normocytic red cells with no blasts, tear drops or fragments, bilirubin 8 micromol/L (less than 20), direct antiglobulin test negative, ferritin 46 micrograms/L (20 to 100)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Transfuse packed red cells over four hours and recheck the full blood count the following morning before discharge
options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for children who are haemodynamically compromised, symptomatic at rest or still falling, because in this condition spontaneous recovery is the rule and transfusion exposes the child to sensitisation without changing the course. A boy who is running about with a compensated circulation does not meet that threshold. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on anaemia in children)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on anaemia in children

options.text: Commence oral elemental iron daily, reduce his cow milk intake, and repeat the full blood count in four weeks
options.rationale: Iron deficiency produces microcytosis with a low ferritin and a raised red cell distribution width, whereas this boy has normocytic cells with a ferritin in the normal range. Iron will not correct an anaemia caused by temporary failure of red cell production. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on iron deficiency)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on iron deficiency

options.text: Arrange a bone marrow aspirate and trephine with cytogenetics through the paediatric oncology service this week
options.rationale: Marrow examination is indicated when more than one lineage is affected, when blasts or tear drop cells appear on the film, or when there is organomegaly, lymphadenopathy or bone pain, and none of those are present. An isolated normocytic anaemia with a low reticulocyte count and otherwise normal counts is investigated by serial monitoring first. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on anaemia in children)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on anaemia in children

options.text: Give intravenous immunoglobulin over two days and arrange haematology review once the infusions have been completed
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin is used for parvovirus associated red cell aplasia in immunocompromised children with persistent viraemia, not for the self limiting post viral aplasia of an immunocompetent toddler. Giving it here adds risk and cost without changing the natural history. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Pure red cell aplasia)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Pure red cell aplasia

options.text: Repeat the full blood count with a reticulocyte count in one week and review him then with clear return advice
options.rationale: Transient erythroblastopenia of childhood follows a viral illness in a previously well toddler and recovers spontaneously over four to eight weeks, heralded by a rising reticulocyte count that is the single most informative repeat measurement. Serial counts also protect against the alternative diagnoses by revealing any evolving cytopenia in another lineage. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on anaemia in children)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on anaemia in children

explanation.summary: Transient erythroblastopenia of childhood is an acquired pure red cell aplasia that typically affects children between six months and four years, often several weeks after a viral illness, and it resolves spontaneously within one to two months. The blood picture is an isolated normocytic anaemia with a strikingly low reticulocyte count and normal white cell and platelet counts, with a normal blood film. Its two important mimics are iron deficiency, which is microcytic with a low ferritin, and Diamond Blackfan anaemia, which presents in the first year with macrocytosis, raised fetal haemoglobin and often thumb or craniofacial anomalies. Leukaemia is excluded clinically and on the film by the absence of blasts, additional cytopenias, organomegaly and bone pain. Management is observation with serial counts, and transfusion is reserved for the child who is symptomatic at rest or haemodynamically compromised because most children compensate remarkably well even at low haemoglobin levels reached slowly.
key_points: Isolated normocytic anaemia with reticulocytopenia and normal other lineages after a viral illness is the defining pattern.
A rising reticulocyte count on a repeat sample confirms recovery and is the key follow up measurement.
Normal ferritin with normocytic indices excludes iron deficiency as the cause.
Diamond Blackfan anaemia presents earlier, with macrocytosis, raised fetal haemoglobin and congenital anomalies.
Transfusion is decided on symptoms and haemodynamics rather than on a haemoglobin threshold alone.
explanation.pearls: Anaemia that develops over weeks is tolerated far better than the same haemoglobin reached acutely, so a toddler with a haemoglobin in the 60s who is playing normally with a normal blood pressure and no tachypnoea can usually be watched with serial counts rather than transfused.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on anaemia in children
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on iron deficiency
BMJ Best Practice: Pure red cell aplasia
